props.title: Rivers and Tides
props.initialSlug: Documentary about environmental artist Andy Goldsworthy

sections.content: Rivers and Tides revolutionized how documentary film captures environmental art. Following Scottish artist Andy Goldsworthy, director Thomas Riedelsheimer creates a mesmerizing portrait of ephemeral art that mirrors nature's own cycles. The film's patient observation of Goldsworthy's meticulous process - building delicate ice sculptures at dawn, weaving elaborate driftwood structures that float away with the tide - established a new visual language for documenting site-specific art. This influenced later artistic documentaries like Gregory Crewdson: Brief Encounters (2012) and Leaning Into the Wind (2017), Riedelsheimer's second collaboration with Goldsworthy.

sections.content: The film's revolutionary approach to capturing artistic process influenced a wave of contemplative documentaries about artists' relationship with nature. Mountain (2017) adopted similar patient observation techniques to explore humanity's complex relationship with peaks and heights. Aquarela (2018) pushed the technical boundaries even further, filming water in its various forms at 96 frames-per-second to create an immersive portrait of Earth's most abundant element. SUBHEAD: Nature as Creative Collaborator

Rivers and Tides established a distinct subgenre of art documentaries where nature itself becomes a creative force. Unlike traditional artist profiles, the film shows Goldsworthy embracing failure as tides wash away his work or wind collapses delicate structures. This influenced later works like Walking with Giants: The Grizzlies of Siberia (2020) and The Ancient Woods (2017), which similarly blur lines between environmental documentary and art film. The patience required to capture these moments - waiting for ice to melt or leaves to scatter - created a new template for observational filmmaking.
